title: The Grateful Tartaro and the Heren-Suge
subtitle: A ball-game bargain frees a prisoner

learningObjectives.text: What does the grateful Tartaro give?

ball.author: Basque storytellers; collected and translated by Wentworth Webster
ball.translator: Wentworth Webster, with assistance from Julien Vinson and other local contributors
ball.locator: THE GRATEFUL TARTARO AND THE HEREN-SUGE.; THE GRATEFUL TARTARO AND THE HEREN-SUGE., normalized characters 480-1491
ball.excerpt: The next day the two sons of the king were playing at ball against (the wall of) the stable where the Tartaro was confined, and the ball went into the stable. One of the boys goes and asks the Tartaro-- "Throw me back my ball, I beg you." He says to him, "Yes, if you will deliver me." He replies, "Yes, yes," and he threw him the ball. A moment after, the ball goes again to the Tartaro. He asks for it again; and the Tartaro says: "If you will deliver me, I will give it you." The boy says, "Yes, yes," takes his ball, and goes off. The ball goes there for the third time, but the Tartaro will not give it before he is let out. The boy says that he has not the key. The Tartaro says to him: "Go to your mother, and tell her to look in your right ear, because something hurts you there. Your mother will have the key in her left pocket, and take it out." The boy goes, and does as the Tartaro had told him. He takes the key from his mother, and delivers the Tartaro. When he was letting him go, he said to him:
ball.note: Verbatim English text from Webster's second edition, collected chiefly in Labourd. The collection distinguishes local tales from French-derived contes des fées and compares some motifs with wider European stories.

narrativeBlocks.title: A kindness returned
narrativeBlocks.body: Not every Tartaro tale ends in a chase: in this one, a man does the ogre a service — frees him or spares him — and the Tartaro is grateful, and gratitude in these tales always means a gift.

narrativeBlocks.title: The rolling ball
narrativeBlocks.body: The grateful Tartaro gives a magic ball — roll it ahead of you and it leads to whatever you most need, even through paths no man could find.

narrativeBlocks.title: The seven-headed serpent
narrativeBlocks.body: The ball leads to where the Heren-Suge — the terrible seven-headed serpent of the Basque tales — holds its captive or its hoard. Heads regrow if struck carelessly; the fight is a puzzle.

narrativeBlocks.title: The serpent overcome
narrativeBlocks.body: The hero defeats the Heren-Suge the way all such beasts fall in the tales — with the right method, the right tool, or the ogre's own gift showing the way. The gift completes its work.

narrativeBlocks.title: The kind ogre's role
narrativeBlocks.body: The Labourd Tartaro is double-faced: devourer of the careless, benefactor of the courteous. Which ogre you meet depends on how you treat the strange being on the road.

quiz.prompt: What does the grateful Tartaro give the hero?

choices.text: A key to the mountain's treasure
A magic ball that rolls ahead and leads to whatever he most needs
An ointment that makes him invisible

quiz.explanation: The rolling ball is the guide-gift — follow it, and the quest finds its way.

choices.text: The Basque seven-headed serpent — heads that regrow unless slain the right way
The wild man of the woods
A giant who guards the passes

quiz.explanation: The multi-headed serpent — the Basque Hydra.
